segments.text: This Roman cup turns from green to red.

visual.label: The Lycurgus Cup, lit from the front (British Museum)

segments.text: Lit from the front, the glass looks a dull, opaque green.
Lit from behind, it glows red.
It's the Lycurgus Cup, made around the year 300.

visual.label: The Lycurgus Cup, Late Roman, about 300 AD (British Museum)

segments.text: Its carved glass shows King Lycurgus, trapped by a vine.
For centuries, scientists couldn't explain the colours.
Then, in 1990, researchers put broken fragments of the glass under a powerful microscope.
Inside were specks of silver and gold, as small as fifty nanometres.
Silver reflects the green. Gold gives the red glow.

visual.title: THE TRICK
visual.evidence: Kool et al., Beilstein J. Nanotechnol. (2020)

segments.text: Roman glassmakers pulled it off more than sixteen centuries before science could explain it.

title: This Roman cup turns from green to red, and it took until 1990 to know why #history
description: Lit from the front, the 4th-century Lycurgus Cup looks green; lit from behind, it glows red. In 1990 scientists traced the effect to tiny particles of silver and gold in the glass.
sources: British Museum, "Discover the Lycurgus Cup" (Google Arts & Culture): https://artsandculture.google.com/story/discover-the-lycurgus-cup/mwWBqnUNwgBpLQ?hl=en

Kool, L. et al. (2020). Gold and silver dichroic nanocomposite in the quest for 3D printing the Lycurgus cup. Beilstein Journal of Nanotechnology 11: 16-23. https://www.beilstein-journals.org/bjnano/articles/11/2
